Interfaces

AuthProfile

The full profile object stored in the manager.

KeyResult

Returned by getKey() — contains everything you need to make an API call and report back.

AuthProfileManagerConfig

Configuration options passed to the manager.

Key Rotation Logic

When you call getKey(provider), the selection algorithm runs:

  1. Filter by provider — Only profiles matching the requested provider
  2. Filter enabled — Skip profiles where enabled === false
  3. Filter cooldown — Skip profiles where Date.now() < cooldownUntil
  4. Sort by priority — Highest priority number first
  5. Round-robin within tier — Among profiles with the same priority, rotate usage evenly

This means your highest-priority keys are always preferred, but if they’re all in cooldown, lower-priority fallbacks pick up automatically.

Rate Limit Handling

Exponential Backoff

When markRateLimited() is called, cooldown duration increases exponentially:

Consecutive FailuresCooldown DurationFormula
1st failure60 seconds2^0 × 60,000ms
2nd failure120 seconds2^1 × 60,000ms
3rd failure240 seconds2^2 × 60,000ms
4th failure300 seconds (capped)2^3 × 60,000ms → capped at maxCooldownMs
5th+ failure300 seconds (capped)Stays at cap until markSuccess()

Calling markSuccess() resets failureCount to 0, so the next failure starts fresh at 60 seconds.

Practical Usage Pattern

Caution

The recursive retry above has no depth limit. In production, add a max-retry counter or use getAvailableProfiles() to check remaining capacity before retrying.

Multi-Provider Setup

Manage keys across all your providers independently:

Each provider’s key pool is managed independently — an OpenAI cooldown doesn’t affect your Anthropic keys.

Events

The auth profile manager emits events through the kernel’s event system. Use these for monitoring and alerting.

EventEmitted WhenPayload
auth.profile.addedProfile registered{ provider, label, priority }
auth.profile.removedProfile deleted{ provider, label }
auth.profile.cooldownRate limit detected{ provider, label, cooldownMs, failureCount }
auth.profile.enabledProfile re-enabled{ provider, label }
auth.profile.disabledProfile disabled{ provider, label }

Listening to Events

Best Practices

  1. Use descriptive labels — Include team member names, environment, or purpose: 'alice-prod', 'shared-dev', 'billing-account-2'

  2. Set priority by rate limit tier — Keys with higher rate limits should get higher priority numbers so they’re used first

  3. Monitor cooldown events — If auth.profile.cooldown fires frequently, you need more keys or should reduce throughput

  4. Prefer setEnabled(false) over remove() — Disabling preserves the profile for re-activation. Only remove when a key is permanently revoked

  5. Keep redundancy per provider — At least 2 profiles per critical provider ensures one is always available during cooldown

  6. Report outcomes consistently — Always call markSuccess() or markRateLimited() after every API call. Missing reports break the rotation logic

  7. Load keys at startup — Register all profiles immediately after kernel.start() so they’re available before the first request

Limitations & Notes

  • In-memory only — Profiles are not persisted to SQLite. They must be re-added after every kernel restart. If you need persistence, store keys in your own database and load them at startup.

  • Not auto-wired to ModelRouter — The auth profiles module is standalone. You can integrate it with custom provider calls, but the built-in ModelRouter does not yet pull keys from it automatically.

  • No encryption at rest — API keys are stored as plain strings in memory. Ensure your hosting environment is secured and avoid logging profile objects.

  • Cooldown is wall-clock based — If the kernel restarts, all cooldowns are cleared (since they’re in memory). This is generally fine — if a key was rate-limited before restart, it likely has capacity again.

  • Single-key scenarios — If you only have one key per provider, use the standard environment variable approach (OPENAI_API_KEY, etc.). Auth profiles add value at 2+ keys.
Polling monitors that run at configurable intervals — health checks, inbox polling, data sync, and periodic automation.

Background loops are continuous polling monitors that execute a function at a fixed interval, inspect the result, and optionally submit an intent or trigger an agent when something actionable is detected. They form the backbone of any autonomous system that needs to watch external state — inboxes, APIs, databases, queues — without relying on webhooks or push notifications.

How loops differ from scheduled jobs

ConcernBackground LoopsScheduler
TimingFixed-interval polling (every n ms)Cron expressions or one-shot delays
StateContext threaded between ticksStateless per execution
Trigger conditionNon-null return from monitor functionTime-based (cron match)
PurposeContinuous monitoring with memoryTimed, fire-and-forget actions
ExamplesHealth checks, inbox polling, price trackingDaily reports, hourly cleanup

Use background loops when you need to repeatedly check something and react when conditions change. Use the scheduler when you need something to happen at a specific time.

Common use cases

  • Health monitoring — ping an endpoint every 30 seconds, alert on failure
  • Inbox polling — check for new emails, tickets, or messages
  • Cache warming — refresh hot data before it expires
  • Data sync — pull changes from an external system periodically
  • Queue draining — process items from a work queue in controlled batches

Quick start

When monitor returns a non-null value, the loop submits the configured target (an intent in this case) with the result attached as context. When it returns null, nothing happens and the next tick is scheduled.

API reference

All methods are available on kernel.loops.

register(input: BackgroundLoopInput): BackgroundLoopDef

Registers a new background loop and immediately starts polling.

pause(loopId: string): void

Stops polling for the specified loop. State is preserved and the paused status is persisted to SQLite.

resume(loopId: string): void

Resumes a paused loop. Context is reset to null and polling starts fresh.

remove(loopId: string): void

Permanently removes a loop. Clears the timer, deletes persisted metadata, and emits loop.removed.

list(): BackgroundLoopDef[]

Returns all registered loops with their current state.

BackgroundLoopInput

Constraints:

  • intervalMs must be between 1,000 (1 second) and 86,400,000 (24 hours)
  • name is required and must be a non-empty string
  • Duplicate id values throw a ValidationError
  • target is optional — if omitted, the loop tracks state but never submits actions

How it works

setTimeout chaining (no drift)

Background loops use setTimeout chaining rather than setInterval. Each tick schedules the next tick only after the current monitor function completes. This eliminates timer drift — if a monitor takes 2 seconds to execute on a 10-second interval, the next tick fires 10 seconds after completion, not 8 seconds later.

Tick lifecycle

Error handling

If the monitor function throws, the loop does not crash. Instead:

  1. The error is logged
  2. A loop.error event is emitted with { loopId, name, error }
  3. Context is preserved from the previous successful tick
  4. The next tick is scheduled normally

This makes loops resilient to transient failures like network timeouts or API rate limits.

Context threading

The return value of each tick is passed as the argument to the next tick. This lets monitors maintain state across invocations without external storage.

The actionability rule

The rule is simple but critical:

If monitor returns anything other than null or undefined, it is treated as actionable and the configured target is triggered.

This means you cannot use the return value for both state tracking and conditional triggering without additional structure.

Problem: naive state tracking triggers every tick

The monitor always returns currentPrice (a number), so the target fires on every single tick — not just when the 5% threshold is crossed.

Solution: separate state from signal

Use a wrapper object to carry state, and return null when no action is needed:

Wait — returning null means we lose context. The next tick receives null and can’t compare prices.

Best solution: use a closure for persistent state

This cleanly separates state management (the closure) from action signaling (the return value).

Patterns

Pattern 1: Health monitor

Triggers only on failure. Returns null when the service is healthy.

Pattern 2: Inbox poller with cursor

Uses context threading to track the last processed item. Triggers when new items are found.

Note: every time new tickets exist, the return value is non-null, so the target is triggered. This is intentional — you want to process tickets as they arrive. The context threading (last ticket ID) ensures you never re-process old tickets.

Pattern 3: Periodic data sync (always triggers)

When you want the action to fire on every tick unconditionally, always return a non-null value.

Pattern 4: Conditional with closure state

Combines external state tracking with selective triggering.

Pause and resume

pause(loopId)

  • Clears the active timer (no more ticks fire)
  • Preserves the loop definition and metadata
  • Persists state: 'paused' to SQLite
  • Emits loop.paused event

resume(loopId)

  • Resets context to null (fresh start)
  • Schedules the first tick immediately
  • Persists state: 'active' to SQLite
  • Emits loop.resumed event

Use pause/resume instead of remove when the loop will be needed again. Removing a loop deletes all metadata — resuming simply picks up where the definition left off (with a fresh context).

Lifecycle and persistence

Startup (kernel.start())

  1. Opens the SQLite store
  2. Loads persisted loop definitions (id, name, intervalMs, state)
  3. Loops in active state wait for their monitor function to be re-registered
  4. Loops in paused state remain paused

Re-registration on restart

Monitor functions are JavaScript code — they cannot be serialized to SQLite. After a restart, you must call register() again for each loop. If a persisted loop with the same ID already exists, the registration reattaches the monitor function and resumes polling.

Shutdown (kernel.stop())

  1. Clears all active timers
  2. Persists current loop states to SQLite
  3. Closes the store connection

No data is lost during graceful shutdown.

Events

Background loops emit events through the kernel’s event system.

EventEmitted whenPayload
loop.pausedLoop is paused{ loopId, name }
loop.resumedLoop is resumed{ loopId, name }
loop.removedLoop is permanently deleted{ loopId, name }
loop.errorMonitor function threw an error{ loopId, name, error }
loop.action.triggeredMonitor returned an actionable result{ loopId, name, result, target }
loop.action.failedTarget execution failed{ loopId, name, error, result }

Listening to events

Validation rules

RuleConstraint
intervalMs minimum1,000 ms (1 second)
intervalMs maximum86,400,000 ms (24 hours)
Duplicate IDsThrows ValidationError
name requiredMust be a non-empty string
monitor requiredMust be a function

Validation runs synchronously during register(). Invalid inputs throw immediately — no loop is created.

Best practices

  1. Keep monitors fast. Avoid CPU-heavy work or long-running I/O inside the monitor. If processing is expensive, return the data and let the target handle it.

  2. Return null for “nothing to do.” This prevents unnecessary intent submissions and keeps your system quiet when there’s nothing actionable.

  3. Use closures for state that shouldn’t trigger actions. When you need to track values across ticks without firing the target every time, store state in a closure variable and only return non-null when you actually want to trigger.

  4. Handle errors inside the monitor when possible. While the loop won’t crash on unhandled errors, catching them yourself gives you finer control over retry logic and error reporting.

  5. Use pause/resume over remove. If a loop will be needed again (maintenance windows, temporary disablement), pause it. Removing deletes all metadata.

  6. Use context threading for cursor-based polling. When polling a database or API with pagination, return the last-seen ID or cursor — the next tick receives it automatically.

  7. Set intervals appropriate to the data source. Don’t poll an API every second if it only updates every minute. Respect rate limits and be a good citizen.

  8. Monitor the loop.error event. Repeated errors from a loop may indicate a configuration issue or a downstream service that’s permanently down.

Problem: naive state tracking triggers every tick
Best solution: use a closure for persistent state

Sandbox Enforcement

The sandbox is Kernova’s primary defense against filesystem and shell abuse by AI agents. It constrains all file and shell operations to a single directory tree.

How It Works

  1. Resolution: All paths are resolved relative to sandboxDir using path.resolve(sandboxDir, userPath).
  2. Normalization: The resolved path is normalized to remove ., .., and redundant separators.
  3. Containment check: The normalized path must startsWith(sandboxDir). If not → blocked.

Using Tools in Agents

Pattern 1: Let the LLM Decide (Automatic)

When an agent has tools available and you don’t provide a custom executor, the default executor calls completeWithTools(). This sends tool definitions to the LLM as part of the prompt, and the LLM decides whether (and which) tools to invoke in a multi-turn loop.

This is the most common pattern. The LLM sees the tool descriptions in its context and calls them as part of its reasoning loop.

Pattern 2: Direct Invocation (Custom Executor)

When you need deterministic control over tool usage — specific order, conditional logic, or combining tool results before the LLM sees them — use a custom executor with tools.useTool():

Pattern 3: Hybrid (LLM + Direct)

You can mix both approaches. Use direct calls for setup/teardown, and let the LLM handle the creative middle:

The enable/disable system follows a clear priority order:

  1. disabled array (highest priority): If a tool ID appears in disabled, it is removed regardless of the enabled array.
  2. enabled array: If set, only tools in this list are available. Everything else is excluded.
  3. Neither set (default): All 6 tools are registered and available.

Connect Kernova to external messaging platforms — Webhook, WebSocket, and platform-specific adapters for Slack, Discord, and more.

Channels are bidirectional bridges between Kernova and external messaging platforms. Inbound messages are normalized into a common format and dispatched as intents; outbound responses flow back to the originating channel for delivery.

## Overview

The channel system provides a unified interface for connecting Kernova to any messaging platform — from simple webhook endpoints to persistent WebSocket connections to third-party chat platforms.

**Two general-purpose adapters:**

- **WebhookChannelAdapter** — HTTP POST-based ingestion for server-to-server integrations
- **WebSocketChannelAdapter** — Persistent bidirectional connections for real-time communication

**Five platform-specific adapters — fully implemented:**

- **SlackAdapter** — Slack Web API + Events API with signature verification
- **DiscordAdapter** — Discord Gateway WebSocket + REST API with heartbeat/resume
- **TelegramAdapter** — Bot API with long-polling or webhook mode
- **WhatsAppAdapter** — Meta Cloud API with webhook verification
- **EmailAdapter** — Raw SMTP sending + IMAP polling for receiving

**SDK integration** is designed for minimal boilerplate:

```typescript
app.channel('incoming', adapter);   // Register a channel
app.onMessage(async (msg) => {});   // Handle inbound messages
```

Under the hood, the **ConnectorRegistry** manages all adapters — handling registration, reconnection logic, message normalization, and routing.

## Architecture

```
External Platform ←→ Channel Adapter ←→ ConnectorRegistry ←→ EventBus → Kernel (Intent)
```

### Inbound Flow

1. A message arrives at the platform (HTTP POST, WebSocket frame, Slack event, etc.)
2. The channel adapter normalizes it into a standard `InboundMessage`
3. The `ConnectorRegistry` validates the message structure
4. An event `channel.message.received` is emitted on the EventBus
5. Registered message handlers are invoked
6. Optionally, the message is submitted as an intent to the Kernel for agent processing

### Outbound Flow

1. An agent produces a response (or the application sends one programmatically)
2. The `ConnectorRegistry` routes the message to the correct adapter by connector ID
3. The adapter's `send()` method serializes and delivers it to the platform
4. A `channel.message.sent` or `channel.message.failed` event is emitted

## Quick Start with SDK

```typescript
import { Kernova } from '@kernova/sdk';
import { WebhookChannelAdapter } from '@kernova/core';

const app = await Kernova.create();

// Register a webhook channel
app.channel('incoming', new WebhookChannelAdapter({ port: 3100, path: '/hooks' }));

// Handle all inbound messages
app.onMessage(async (msg) => {
  console.log(`[${msg.channel}] ${msg.sender}: ${msg.content}`);
});

await app.serve(); // Starts listening on configured ports
```

That's it — messages POSTed to `http://localhost:3100/hooks` are normalized and delivered to your handler.

## WebhookChannelAdapter

The webhook adapter starts a lightweight HTTP server and accepts inbound messages as JSON POST requests. It's the simplest path to production for server-to-server integrations.

### Configuration

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `port` | `number` | `3100` | HTTP server port |
| `path` | `string` | `'/webhook'` | URL path to accept POST requests |
| `id` | `string` | auto-generated | Unique connector identifier |

### Behavior

- Starts an HTTP server bound to the configured port
- Accepts **POST** requests at the configured path with a JSON body
- Responds immediately with `200 OK` and `{ received: true, messageId }` — processing is asynchronous
- Returns `404` for non-POST methods or mismatched paths
- Returns `400` for missing/invalid JSON body

### Usage

```typescript
import { WebhookChannelAdapter } from '@kernova/core';

const webhook = new WebhookChannelAdapter({
  port: 3100,
  path: '/incoming',
});

// Register with the core ConnectorRegistry
kernel.channels.register({
  channelType: 'webhook',
  name: 'My Webhook',
  config: { port: 3100, path: '/incoming' },
});

// Or use the SDK shorthand
app.channel('webhooks', webhook);
```

### Expected POST Body

```json
{
  "sender": "user@example.com",
  "content": "Hello, can you help me?",
  "timestamp": "2025-07-10T14:30:00Z"
}
```

| Field | Required | Description |
|-------|----------|-------------|
| `sender` | Yes | Identifier for the message author |
| `content` | Yes | The message text |
| `timestamp` | No | ISO 8601 timestamp (defaults to server time) |

### Response

```json
{
  "received": true,
  "messageId": "msg_a1b2c3d4"
}
```

### Testing with cURL

```bash
curl -X POST http://localhost:3100/incoming \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"sender": "test-user", "content": "Hello from cURL"}'
```

## WebSocketChannelAdapter

The WebSocket adapter maintains persistent bidirectional connections — ideal for real-time user interfaces, chat applications, and dashboards that require instant message delivery.

### Configuration

| Option | Type | Default | Description |
|--------|------|---------|-------------|
| `port` | `number` | `3200` | HTTP/WebSocket server port |
| `path` | `string` | `'/ws'` | WebSocket upgrade path |
| `keepaliveIntervalMs` | `number` | `30000` | Ping interval in milliseconds |

### Behavior

- Starts an HTTP server and upgrades connections to WebSocket at the configured path
- Sends **ping** frames at the configured keepalive interval — terminates clients that don't respond with **pong**
- Supports **multiple concurrent clients** (tracks all active connections)
- `send()` broadcasts to all connected clients
- Inbound messages are expected as JSON: `{ sender?, content }`

### Usage

```typescript
import { WebSocketChannelAdapter } from '@kernova/core';

const ws = new WebSocketChannelAdapter({
  port: 8080,
  path: '/ws',
  keepaliveIntervalMs: 30000,
});

app.channel('realtime', ws);
```

### Client-Side Connection

```javascript
const ws = new WebSocket('ws://localhost:8080/ws');

ws.onopen = () => {
  ws.send(JSON.stringify({ sender: 'user-1', content: 'Hello!' }));
};

ws.onmessage = (event) => {
  const response = JSON.parse(event.data);
  console.log('Response:', response);
};

ws.onclose = () => {
  console.log('Disconnected from server');
};
```

### Keepalive & Connection Management

The adapter automatically pings connected clients every `keepaliveIntervalMs` milliseconds. If a client fails to respond with a pong frame before the next ping cycle, the connection is considered stale and terminated.

This ensures server resources are freed from zombie connections without manual intervention.

## SDK Methods

The SDK provides two primary methods for channel management:

### `app.channel(name, adapter)`

Registers a channel adapter with the application. Returns `this` for chaining.

```typescript
app.channel('hooks', new WebhookChannelAdapter({ port: 3100 }));
```

### `app.onMessage(handler)`

Registers a global handler invoked for **all** inbound messages across all channels. Returns `this` for chaining.

```typescript
app.onMessage(async (msg) => {
  console.log(`Received: ${msg.content}`);
});
```

### Chaining

Both methods return the app instance, enabling fluent configuration:

```typescript
app
  .channel('hooks', new WebhookChannelAdapter({ port: 3100 }))
  .channel('ws', new WebSocketChannelAdapter({ port: 8080 }))
  .onMessage(async (msg) => {
    // This handler receives messages from both channels
    console.log(`[${msg.channel}] ${msg.sender}: ${msg.content}`);
  });
```

## ConnectorRegistry (Core API)

For advanced use cases that bypass the SDK, the `ConnectorRegistry` is available directly on the kernel. It manages the full lifecycle of channel adapters.

### Methods

#### `register(input)`

Registers a new channel adapter with configuration validation.

```typescript
kernel.channels.register({
  channelType: 'webhook',
  name: 'Production Webhook',
  config: { port: 3100, path: '/hooks' },
});
```

#### `connect(connectorId)`

Initiates connection to the platform for the specified connector.

```typescript
await kernel.channels.connect('connector_abc123');
```

#### `disconnect(connectorId)`

Gracefully disconnects from the platform and cancels any pending reconnection attempts.

```typescript
await kernel.channels.disconnect('connector_abc123');
```

#### `send(request)`

Sends an outbound message through the specified connector.

```typescript
await kernel.channels.send({
  connectorId: 'connector_abc123',
  message: { content: 'Hello from Kernova!' },
});
```

#### `status()`

Returns all registered connectors with their current connection state.

```typescript
const connectors = kernel.channels.status();
// [{ id, name, channelType, state: 'connected' | 'disconnected' | 'connecting' | 'failed' }]
```

## Message Types

All channel communication uses these standardized interfaces:

### InboundMessage

```typescript
interface InboundMessage {
  id: string;           // Unique message identifier
  sender: string;       // Author identifier (email, user ID, etc.)
  channel: string;      // Channel name (e.g., 'hooks', 'realtime')
  content: string;      // Message text content
  timestamp: string;    // ISO 8601 timestamp
  connectorId: string;  // Internal connector reference
  raw?: unknown;        // Original platform-specific payload (for advanced processing)
}
```

### OutboundMessage

```typescript
interface OutboundMessage {
  content: string;        // Plain text response
  structured?: unknown;   // Rich content (cards, buttons, embeds, etc.)
}
```

The `structured` field allows platform-specific rich content. Each adapter is responsible for serializing structured content into its platform's format — or falling back to `content` if the platform doesn't support it.

### DeliveryReceipt

```typescript
interface DeliveryReceipt {
  messageId: string;
  delivered: boolean;
  timestamp: string;
  error?: string;
}
```

## Reconnection & Resilience

Channel adapters are designed for production reliability. The `ConnectorRegistry` implements automatic reconnection and graceful degradation.

### Exponential Backoff

On connection failure, the registry retries with exponential backoff:

| Attempt | Delay |
|---------|-------|
| 1 | 1 second |
| 2 | 2 seconds |
| 3 | 4 seconds |
| 4 | 8 seconds |
| 5 | 16 seconds |
| 6+ | 60 seconds (max) |

### State Transitions

```
disconnected → connecting → connected
                    ↓
                 failed → reconnecting → connected
                              ↓
                           failed (retry with backoff)
```

### Behavior Details

- **Explicit disconnect** cancels all pending reconnection attempts — no automatic retry
- **Delivery timeout**: if `send()` takes longer than 30 seconds, it returns a failure receipt
- **Structured content degradation**: if a platform rejects rich content (cards, buttons), the adapter automatically falls back to plain text using the `content` field
- **Connection state** is always queryable via `kernel.channels.status()`

All platform adapters ship fully implemented with `@kernova/core`. No external dependencies needed — they use native `fetch`, `net`, `tls`, `crypto`, and the `ws` library (already bundled).

### Slack Adapter

Connects to Slack using the Web API for sending and the Events API (via HTTP webhook) for receiving. Includes HMAC-SHA256 signature verification.

**Config:**
```typescript
import { SlackAdapter } from '@kernova/core';

const slack = new SlackAdapter({
  type: 'slack',
  botToken: process.env.SLACK_BOT_TOKEN!,    // xoxb-...
  signingSecret: process.env.SLACK_SIGNING_SECRET!,
  port: 3300,           // Webhook server port (optional, default: 3300)
  defaultChannel: 'C0123456789',  // Fallback channel for outbound (optional)
});
```

**Setup steps:**
1. Create a Slack App at [api.slack.com/apps](https://api.slack.com/apps)
2. Enable "Event Subscriptions" and point the Request URL to `http://your-server:3300/`
3. Subscribe to `message.channels` and `message.im` events
4. Install the app to your workspace and copy the Bot Token + Signing Secret

**Features:**
- `auth.test` verification on connect
- Webhook signature verification (timing-safe HMAC-SHA256)
- URL verification challenge (automatic)
- Slack blocks support via `message.structured` (pass an array of block objects)
- Bot message filtering (ignores own messages)
- Channel routing (replies in the same channel the message came from)

**Example:**
```typescript
kernel.channels.register({ channelType: 'slack', name: 'team-slack', config: slackConfig });
await kernel.channels.connect('connector_id');

// Send a message with blocks
await kernel.channels.send({
  connectorId: 'connector_id',
  message: {
    content: 'Deployment successful!',
    structured: [
      { type: 'section', text: { type: 'mrkdwn', text: '*Deploy* completed ✅' } },
      { type: 'actions', elements: [{ type: 'button', text: { type: 'plain_text', text: 'View Logs' } }] },
    ],
  },
});
```

### Email Adapter

Connects to email using raw SMTP for sending and IMAP polling for receiving. Uses Node.js native `net`/`tls` modules — no external email libraries needed.

**Config:**
```typescript
import { EmailAdapter } from '@kernova/core';

const email = new EmailAdapter({
  type: 'email',
  smtpHost: 'smtp.gmail.com',
  smtpPort: 465,
  imapHost: 'imap.gmail.com',
  imapPort: 993,
  username: 'your-bot@gmail.com',
  password: process.env.EMAIL_APP_PASSWORD!,
  useTls: true,
  pollIntervalMs: 60000,       // Check for new mail every 60s
  defaultRecipient: 'team@company.com',  // Fallback send-to address
});
```

**Setup steps:**
1. Create a dedicated email account for the bot
2. Enable IMAP access in your email provider settings
3. For Gmail: generate an App Password (Settings → Security → App Passwords)
4. Provide SMTP and IMAP host/port for your provider

**Features:**
- SMTP client: EHLO → AUTH LOGIN → MAIL FROM → RCPT TO → DATA → QUIT
- IMAP polling: LOGIN → SELECT INBOX → SEARCH UNSEEN → FETCH → STORE +FLAGS (\Seen)
- TLS support for both SMTP and IMAP
- RFC 2822 message formatting
- Auto-reply routing (replies to last sender)
- Polls at configurable interval (caps at 10 messages per poll to avoid overload)

**Example:**
```typescript
kernel.channels.register({ channelType: 'email', name: 'inbox', config: emailConfig });
await kernel.channels.connect('connector_id');

// New emails trigger the message handler
app.onMessage(async (msg) => {
  if (msg.channel === 'email') {
    console.log(`Email from ${msg.sender}: ${msg.content}`);
    // msg.raw contains { subject, uid } for additional context
  }
});

// Reply to the sender
await kernel.channels.send({
  connectorId: 'connector_id',
  message: { content: 'Thanks for your email! I am looking into this.' },
});
```

|----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|-----------|
| Gmail | smtp.gmail.com | 465 | imap.gmail.com | 993 |
| Outlook | smtp-mail.outlook.com | 587 | outlook.office365.com | 993 |
| Yahoo | smtp.mail.yahoo.com | 465 | imap.mail.yahoo.com | 993 |
| Zoho | smtp.zoho.com | 465 | imap.zoho.com | 993 |

### Push Notifications Adapter (FCM/APNs)

Send push notifications to mobile devices. This is **send-only** — push notifications don't have an inbound channel.

**Config:**
```typescript
import { PushAdapter } from '@kernova/core';

// Firebase Cloud Messaging
const push = new PushAdapter({
  type: 'push',
  provider: 'fcm',
  fcmServerKey: process.env.FCM_SERVER_KEY!,
});

// Apple Push Notification Service
const pushApple = new PushAdapter({
  type: 'push',
  provider: 'apns',
  apnsKeyPath: './certs/AuthKey.p8',
  apnsKeyId: 'ABC123DEF4',
  apnsTeamId: 'TEAM123456',
  apnsBundleId: 'com.myapp.ios',
});

app.channel('push', push);
```

**Features:**
- FCM: POST to `https://fcm.googleapis.com/fcm/send` with server key auth
- APNs: HTTP/2 POST with JWT bearer token
- Supports title + body + custom data payload via `message.structured`
- Send-only — `onMessage` is a no-op (mobile devices push back via other channels)
- Delivery receipt indicates success/failure from the push service

**Example — sending a push:**
```typescript
await kernel.channels.send({
  connectorId: 'push-connector-id',
  message: {
    content: 'Your order has shipped!',
    structured: {
      title: 'Order Update',
      body: 'Your order #1234 has shipped and will arrive tomorrow.',
      data: { orderId: '1234', action: 'view_order' },
      deviceToken: 'user-device-token-here',
    },
  },
});
```

### RSS/Atom Feed Adapter

Monitor RSS and Atom feeds for new entries. This is **receive-only** — you can't publish to an RSS feed.

**Config:**
```typescript
import { RssAdapter } from '@kernova/core';

const rss = new RssAdapter({
  type: 'rss',
  feeds: [
    { url: 'https://blog.example.com/feed.xml', name: 'Company Blog' },
    { url: 'https://news.ycombinator.com/rss', name: 'Hacker News' },
    { url: 'https://arxiv.org/rss/cs.AI', name: 'AI Papers' },
  ],
  pollIntervalMs: 300_000,  // Check every 5 minutes
});

app.channel('rss', rss);
```

**Features:**
- Polls configured feed URLs at the specified interval
- Parses XML for `<item>` / `<entry>` elements (supports both RSS 2.0 and Atom)
- Extracts title, link, description/summary, and GUID
- Tracks seen GUIDs to avoid duplicate processing
- New items are dispatched as inbound messages
- Receive-only — `send()` returns an error

**Example — reacting to new articles:**
```typescript
app.onMessage(async (msg) => {
  if (msg.channel === 'rss') {
    console.log(`New article from ${msg.sender}: ${msg.content}`);
    // msg.raw contains { title, link, description, guid, feedName }
    await app.ask(`Summarize this article: ${msg.raw.link}`);
  }
});
```

## Custom Adapter

Building your own channel adapter is straightforward. Implement the `SDKChannelAdapter` interface:

```typescript
import type {
  SDKChannelAdapter,
  InboundMessage,
  OutboundMessage,
  DeliveryReceipt,
} from '@kernova/types';

class MyCustomAdapter implements SDKChannelAdapter {
  readonly id = 'my-adapter';
  readonly type = 'custom';

  private handler?: (msg: InboundMessage) => Promise<void>;

  async connect(): Promise<void> {
    // Initialize your connection (open sockets, start polling, etc.)
    console.log('Custom adapter connected');
  }

  async disconnect(): Promise<void> {
    // Clean up resources
    console.log('Custom adapter disconnected');
  }

  async send(message: OutboundMessage): Promise<DeliveryReceipt> {
    // Deliver the message to your platform
    const messageId = `msg_${Date.now()}`;

    try {
      // ... your delivery logic here
      return { messageId, delivered: true, timestamp: new Date().toISOString() };
    } catch (error) {
      return {
        messageId,
        delivered: false,
        timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
        error: String(error),
      };
    }
  }

  onMessage(handler: (msg: InboundMessage) => Promise<void>): void {
    this.handler = handler;
  }

  // Call this internally when your platform delivers a message
  protected async receiveMessage(sender: string, content: string): Promise<void> {
    if (!this.handler) return;

    await this.handler({
      id: `msg_${Date.now()}`,
      sender,
      channel: this.type,
      content,
      timestamp: new Date().toISOString(),
      connectorId: this.id,
    });
  }
}
```

Register it like any other adapter:

```typescript
app.channel('custom', new MyCustomAdapter());
```

## Events

The channel system emits events on the kernel's EventBus at every significant lifecycle point:

| Event | Emitted When | Payload |
|-------|--------------|---------|
| `channel.message.received` | Inbound message arrives | `{ messageId, sender, channelType }` |
| `channel.message.sent` | Outbound successfully delivered | `{ messageId, recipient }` |
| `channel.message.failed` | Outbound delivery failed | `{ messageId, reason }` |
| `channel.connected` | Adapter establishes connection | `{ name, channelType }` |
| `channel.disconnected` | Adapter disconnects | `{ name }` |
| `channel.connection.failed` | Connection attempt fails | `{ name, reason }` |

### Subscribing to Events

```typescript
kernel.events.on('channel.message.received', (data) => {
  console.log(`New message from ${data.sender} via ${data.channelType}`);
});

kernel.events.on('channel.connection.failed', (data) => {
  console.error(`Channel "${data.name}" failed: ${data.reason}`);
  // Alert your monitoring system
});
```

## Best Practices

### Choosing the Right Adapter

- **Webhook** — Best for server-to-server integrations: CI/CD notifications, API callbacks, third-party service events. Stateless and simple.
- **WebSocket** — Best for real-time user interfaces: chat applications, live dashboards, collaborative tools. Persistent and low-latency.

### Security

- **Validate sender identity** in production. Raw webhook payloads can be spoofed — verify signatures, tokens, or IP allowlists.
- **Use HTTPS (TLS)** in front of webhook adapters. Deploy behind a reverse proxy (nginx, Caddy) or load balancer that terminates TLS.
- **Authenticate WebSocket connections** via a token in the initial handshake or first message. Don't assume all connected clients are trusted.

### Reliability

- **Monitor `channel.connection.failed` events** to detect connectivity issues early. Wire these to your alerting system.
- **Set appropriate keepalive intervals** for WebSocket. Too aggressive (< 10s) wastes bandwidth; too relaxed (> 60s) delays stale connection detection.
- **Handle delivery failures** gracefully. Check the `DeliveryReceipt` from `send()` and implement retry logic for critical messages.

### Scaling

- Each webhook adapter binds to its own port. In production, use a single reverse proxy that routes paths to the appropriate adapter.
- WebSocket adapters track all connected clients in memory. For horizontal scaling, use a shared pub/sub layer (Redis, NATS) to broadcast messages across instances.
- Use the `raw` field on `InboundMessage` to preserve platform-specific metadata that might be needed for advanced routing or auditing.

Channels are bidirectional bridges between Kernova and external messaging platforms. Inbound messages are normalized into a common format and dispatched as intents; outbound responses flow back to the originating channel for delivery.

Overview

The channel system provides a unified interface for connecting Kernova to any messaging platform — from simple webhook endpoints to persistent WebSocket connections to third-party chat platforms.

Two general-purpose adapters:

  • WebhookChannelAdapter — HTTP POST-based ingestion for server-to-server integrations
  • WebSocketChannelAdapter — Persistent bidirectional connections for real-time communication

Five platform-specific adapters — fully implemented:

  • SlackAdapter — Slack Web API + Events API with signature verification
  • DiscordAdapter — Discord Gateway WebSocket + REST API with heartbeat/resume
  • TelegramAdapter — Bot API with long-polling or webhook mode
  • WhatsAppAdapter — Meta Cloud API with webhook verification
  • EmailAdapter — Raw SMTP sending + IMAP polling for receiving

SDK integration is designed for minimal boilerplate:

Under the hood, the ConnectorRegistry manages all adapters — handling registration, reconnection logic, message normalization, and routing.

Architecture

Inbound Flow

  1. A message arrives at the platform (HTTP POST, WebSocket frame, Slack event, etc.)
  2. The channel adapter normalizes it into a standard InboundMessage
  3. The ConnectorRegistry validates the message structure
  4. An event channel.message.received is emitted on the EventBus
  5. Registered message handlers are invoked
  6. Optionally, the message is submitted as an intent to the Kernel for agent processing

Outbound Flow

  1. An agent produces a response (or the application sends one programmatically)
  2. The ConnectorRegistry routes the message to the correct adapter by connector ID
  3. The adapter’s send() method serializes and delivers it to the platform
  4. A channel.message.sent or channel.message.failed event is emitted

Quick Start with SDK

That’s it — messages POSTed to http://localhost:3100/hooks are normalized and delivered to your handler.

WebSocketChannelAdapter

The WebSocket adapter maintains persistent bidirectional connections — ideal for real-time user interfaces, chat applications, and dashboards that require instant message delivery.

  • Sends ping frames at the configured keepalive interval — terminates clients that don’t respond with pong

  • send() broadcasts to all connected clients

Usage

Client-Side Connection

Keepalive & Connection Management

The adapter automatically pings connected clients every keepaliveIntervalMs milliseconds. If a client fails to respond with a pong frame before the next ping cycle, the connection is considered stale and terminated.

This ensures server resources are freed from zombie connections without manual intervention.

Channel adapters are designed for production reliability. The ConnectorRegistry implements automatic reconnection and graceful degradation.

Layered runtime configuration and declarative agent config files — YAML/JSON parsing, inheritance, hot-reload, and environment variable overrides.

Kernova's config system has two distinct subsystems that work together to configure your application at runtime and define agents declaratively.

| Subsystem | Purpose | Package |
|-----------|---------|---------|
| **ConfigManager** | Layered runtime configuration with dot-path access, env overrides, change watching | `@kernova/core` |
| **Agent Config Loader** | YAML/JSON agent definition files with inheritance, validation, discovery, hot-reload | `@kernova/core` |

---

## Overview

**Runtime configuration** (`ConfigManager`) handles your application's settings — model provider, ports, budgets, feature flags. It resolves values through a priority chain: hardcoded defaults → file config → environment variables → programmatic overrides. Any layer can be changed at runtime, and watchers fire when values change.

**Agent config files** are declarative `.agent.yaml` / `.agent.yml` / `.agent.json` files that define agents without writing TypeScript. They support `extends` inheritance, are validated on load, and can be hot-reloaded during development. The CLI's `kernova serve --watch` picks up changes automatically.

Both systems are exported from `@kernova/core`:

```typescript
import {
  ConfigManager,
  parseAgentConfigFile,
  loadAgentConfigWithExtends,
  discoverAgentConfigFiles,
  AgentConfigError,
} from '@kernova/core';
```

---

## Runtime Configuration (ConfigManager)

### Layer Priority

ConfigManager resolves values through four layers, highest priority first:

| Priority | Layer | Source | Typical Use |
|----------|-------|--------|-------------|
| 1 (highest) | `runtime` | Set programmatically via `.set()` | Feature flags, temporary overrides |
| 2 | `env` | Environment variables with `KERNOVA_` prefix | Secrets, deployment-specific values |
| 3 | `file` | Loaded from `kernova.config.json` | Project defaults, shared team settings |
| 4 (lowest) | `defaults` | Hardcoded in code | Safe fallbacks |

When you call `.get('models.default.provider')`, ConfigManager checks each layer top-to-bottom and returns the first defined value.

### Initialization

ConfigManager is created by the kernel during startup. You can also instantiate it directly:

```typescript
import { ConfigManager } from '@kernova/core';
import { EventBus } from '@kernova/core';

const eventBus = new EventBus();

const configManager = new ConfigManager(eventBus, {
  defaults: {
    models: { default: { provider: 'openai', model: 'gpt-4o' } },
    gateway: { port: 3000 },
  },
  fileConfig: loadedFromDisk, // parsed JSON object
  envPrefix: 'KERNOVA_',     // default prefix
});
```

### API Reference

#### `get<T>(path): T | undefined`

Resolve a value through all layers using dot-path notation.

```typescript
const provider = kernel.configManager.get<string>('models.default.provider');
// Returns: 'openai' (from whichever layer has it at highest priority)

const missing = kernel.configManager.get<string>('nonexistent.path');
// Returns: undefined
```

#### `getOrDefault<T>(path, defaultValue): T`

Same as `get()` but returns a fallback if no layer has the value.

```typescript
const port = kernel.configManager.getOrDefault('gateway.port', 3000);
// Returns: 3000 if no layer defines gateway.port

const debug = kernel.configManager.getOrDefault('runtime.debug', false);
```

#### `set(path, value): void`

Set a runtime override. This is the highest-priority layer — it wins over env, file, and defaults.

```typescript
kernel.configManager.set('models.default.model', 'gpt-4o-mini');

// Immediately effective
const model = kernel.configManager.get('models.default.model');
// Returns: 'gpt-4o-mini'
```

Setting a value also triggers watchers and emits a `config.changed` event.

#### `reload(fileConfig): void`

Replace the file layer entirely. Useful after detecting a config file change on disk.

```typescript
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';

const updated = JSON.parse(readFileSync('./kernova.config.json', 'utf-8'));
kernel.configManager.reload(updated);
// Diffs previous file config against new one and emits change events
```

After reload, a `config.reloaded` event is emitted with the number of changed paths.

#### `watch(path, callback): () => void`

Subscribe to changes for a specific config path. Returns an unsubscribe function.

```typescript
const unwatch = kernel.configManager.watch('models.default.provider', (newValue) => {
  console.log(`Provider changed to: ${newValue}`);
  // Reinitialize model client, etc.
});

// Later: stop watching
unwatch();
```

Watchers fire when:
- `set()` is called with a new value for that path
- `reload()` is called and the file layer has a different value at that path

#### `getAll(): Record<string, unknown>`

Get the fully merged configuration object (all layers combined, higher priority wins).

```typescript
const allConfig = kernel.configManager.getAll();
console.log(allConfig.models.default.provider); // resolved value
```

### Environment Variable Mapping

Environment variables are mapped to config paths using a prefix and double-underscore nesting:

| Environment Variable | Config Path |
|---------------------|-------------|
| `KERNOVA_MODELS__DEFAULT__PROVIDER` | `models.default.provider` |
| `KERNOVA_GATEWAY__PORT` | `gateway.port` |
| `KERNOVA_RUNTIME__DEBUG` | `runtime.debug` |

**Rules:**
- Prefix: `KERNOVA_` (configurable via `envPrefix` option)
- Nesting separator: `__` (double underscore) → converted to `.` in config paths
- Case: environment variable keys are lowercased after stripping the prefix
- Values: always strings (you may need to parse numbers/booleans yourself)

```bash
# Shell
export KERNOVA_MODELS__DEFAULT__PROVIDER=anthropic
export KERNOVA_MODELS__DEFAULT__MODEL=claude-sonnet-4-20250514
export KERNOVA_GATEWAY__PORT=8080
```

```typescript
// These resolve from the env layer:
kernel.configManager.get('models.default.provider'); // 'anthropic'
kernel.configManager.get('gateway.port');            // '8080' (string!)
```

### Merge Behavior

When `getAll()` merges layers, it uses deep merge for objects and replacement for scalars/arrays:

- **Objects** — recursively merged (keys from higher-priority layers override lower)
- **Scalars** — replaced entirely
- **Arrays** — replaced entirely (not concatenated)

```typescript
// defaults layer:
{ models: { default: { provider: 'openai', model: 'gpt-4o' } } }

// env layer:
{ models: { default: { provider: 'anthropic' } } }

// getAll() result:
{ models: { default: { provider: 'anthropic', model: 'gpt-4o' } } }
//                      ↑ from env              ↑ from defaults
```

## Agent Config Files

Agent config files let you define agents declaratively without writing TypeScript. They're ideal for prompt iteration, non-developer authoring, and version-controlled agent definitions.

### File Format

Agents can be defined in YAML or JSON. The schema is the same for both formats.

#### Full Schema (YAML)

```yaml
name: my-agent                    # Required — unique agent identifier
description: What this agent does # Optional — used in agent selection scoring
instructions: |                   # Required — the system prompt
  You are a helpful assistant.
  Always be concise and accurate.
model: gpt-4o                     # Optional — overrides kernel default model
tools:                            # Optional — tool IDs this agent can access
  - http-fetch
  - web-search
schedules:                        # Optional — time-based triggers
  - name: hourly-check
    cron: "0 * * * *"
    goal: "Run health check"
  - name: delayed-init
    delayMs: 5000
    goal: "Initialize cache"
triggers:                         # Optional — event-based triggers
  - name: on-error
    event: "intent.failed"
    goal: "Investigate failure"
    condition: "event.data.priority === 'critical'"
extends: ./base-agent.agent.yaml  # Optional — inherit from another config
```

#### JSON Equivalent

```json
{
  "name": "my-agent",
  "description": "What this agent does",
  "instructions": "You are a helpful assistant.\nAlways be concise and accurate.",
  "model": "gpt-4o",
  "tools": ["http-fetch", "web-search"],
  "schedules": [
    { "name": "hourly-check", "cron": "0 * * * *", "goal": "Run health check" },
    { "name": "delayed-init", "delayMs": 5000, "goal": "Initialize cache" }
  ],
  "triggers": [
    {
      "name": "on-error",
      "event": "intent.failed",
      "goal": "Investigate failure",
      "condition": "event.data.priority === 'critical'"
    }
  ],
  "extends": "./base-agent.agent.yaml"
}
```

## Config Inheritance (`extends`)

The `extends` field lets an agent config inherit from a base config. This is useful for sharing instructions, model choices, or tool sets across multiple agents.

### How It Works

1. The loader reads the child config file
2. If `extends` is present, it resolves the path relative to the child file's directory
3. The base config is loaded (recursively — bases can extend other bases)
4. The child is merged on top of the base

### Merge Rules

| Field | Behavior |
|-------|----------|
| `name` | Child always wins (required in child) |
| `instructions` | Child always wins (required in child) |
| `description` | Child wins if defined, otherwise base value |
| `model` | Child wins if defined, otherwise base value |
| `tools` | Child **replaces** base (not concatenated) |
| `schedules` | Child **replaces** base (not concatenated) |
| `triggers` | Child **replaces** base (not concatenated) |
| `extends` | Consumed during loading, not propagated to result |

### Example

```yaml
# agents/base.agent.yaml
name: base
instructions: |
  You are part of the Kernova system. Be helpful, accurate, and concise.
model: gpt-4o
tools:
  - http-fetch
  - date-time
```

```yaml
# agents/specialist.agent.yaml
name: specialist
extends: ./base.agent.yaml
description: A specialist agent with custom tools
instructions: |
  You are a specialist agent. Override base behavior with domain expertise.
tools:
  - web-search      # Replaces base tools entirely (http-fetch and date-time are gone)
```

Resolved result for `specialist`:
```typescript
{
  name: 'specialist',
  description: 'A specialist agent with custom tools',
  instructions: 'You are a specialist agent. Override base behavior...',
  model: 'gpt-4o',          // inherited from base
  tools: ['web-search'],     // replaced (not merged)
}
```

### Deep Chains

Inheritance can be chained: A extends B extends C.

```yaml
# base.agent.yaml
name: base
instructions: "Core system prompt."
model: gpt-4o

# mid-tier.agent.yaml
name: mid-tier
extends: ./base.agent.yaml
instructions: "Mid-tier prompt."
tools:
  - web-search

# leaf.agent.yaml
name: leaf
extends: ./mid-tier.agent.yaml
instructions: "Leaf-level prompt."
```

Resolution order: `base` → `mid-tier` → `leaf`. Each layer's defined fields override the previous.

### Circular Detection

If a chain forms a cycle (A extends B extends A), the loader throws an `AgentConfigError`:

```
[AgentConfig] /path/to/a.agent.yaml: Circular extends dependency detected
```

## Parsing & Serialization Functions

The agent config loader exports utility functions for working with config files programmatically.

### `parseAgentConfigFile(filePath)`

Read and parse a config file from disk. Supports `.agent.yaml`, `.agent.yml`, and `.agent.json`.

```typescript
import { parseAgentConfigFile } from '@kernova/core';

const config = parseAgentConfigFile('./agents/researcher.agent.yaml');
console.log(config.name);         // 'researcher'
console.log(config.tools);        // ['web-search', 'http-fetch']
```

Throws `AgentConfigError` if the file doesn't exist, can't be parsed, or fails validation.

### `parseAgentConfigString(content, filePath)`

Parse config from a string. The `filePath` is used for error messages and to determine format (JSON vs YAML).

```typescript
import { parseAgentConfigString } from '@kernova/core';

const yaml = `
name: test-agent
instructions: You are a test agent.
`;

const config = parseAgentConfigString(yaml, 'virtual.agent.yaml');
```

### `validateAgentConfig(data, filePath)`

Validate a plain object against the agent config schema. Returns the typed `AgentConfigFile` if valid.

```typescript
import { validateAgentConfig } from '@kernova/core';

const raw = JSON.parse(someString);
const validated = validateAgentConfig(raw, 'dynamic.agent.json');
// Throws AgentConfigError if invalid
```

### `mergeAgentConfigs(base, child)`

Merge two configs using inheritance rules (child overrides base, arrays replace).

```typescript
import { mergeAgentConfigs } from '@kernova/core';

const base = parseAgentConfigFile('./agents/base.agent.yaml');
const child = parseAgentConfigFile('./agents/child.agent.yaml');

const merged = mergeAgentConfigs(base, child);
// merged.name === child.name
// merged.model === child.model ?? base.model
```

### `loadAgentConfigWithExtends(filePath)`

The all-in-one loader. Parses the file, resolves `extends` chains recursively, and returns the fully merged config.

```typescript
import { loadAgentConfigWithExtends } from '@kernova/core';

const config = loadAgentConfigWithExtends('./agents/specialist.agent.yaml');
// Inherits from base, fully resolved
```

### `serializeAgentConfigToYaml(config)`

Convert an `AgentConfigFile` object back to a YAML string. Omits undefined/empty fields.

```typescript
import { serializeAgentConfigToYaml } from '@kernova/core';

const yaml = serializeAgentConfigToYaml(config);
fs.writeFileSync('./output.agent.yaml', yaml);
```

### `serializeAgentConfigToJson(config)`

Convert an `AgentConfigFile` object to a pretty-printed JSON string.

```typescript
import { serializeAgentConfigToJson } from '@kernova/core';

const json = serializeAgentConfigToJson(config);
fs.writeFileSync('./output.agent.json', json);
```

### `discoverAgentConfigFiles(dirPath)`

Find all agent config files in a directory (non-recursive scan).

```typescript
import { discoverAgentConfigFiles } from '@kernova/core';

const files = discoverAgentConfigFiles('./agents/');
// ['/abs/path/agents/researcher.agent.yaml', '/abs/path/agents/writer.agent.yaml']
```

Returns an empty array if the directory doesn't exist. If passed a single file path that matches agent config extensions, returns that file in an array.

### `isAgentConfigFile(filename)`

Check whether a filename matches recognized agent config extensions.

```typescript
import { isAgentConfigFile } from '@kernova/core';

isAgentConfigFile('researcher.agent.yaml'); // true
isAgentConfigFile('researcher.agent.yml');  // true
isAgentConfigFile('researcher.agent.json'); // true
isAgentConfigFile('researcher.ts');         // false
isAgentConfigFile('config.yaml');           // false
```

### `watchAgentConfigFiles(paths, onChange)`

Watch a set of config file paths for filesystem changes. Also watches parent directories for new files.

```typescript
import { watchAgentConfigFiles, discoverAgentConfigFiles } from '@kernova/core';

const files = discoverAgentConfigFiles('./agents/');

const stop = watchAgentConfigFiles(files, (filePath, event) => {
  console.log(`${event} detected: ${filePath}`);
  // event is 'change' or 'rename'
});

// Later: stop watching
stop();
```

## File Discovery & Extensions

### Recognized Extensions

| Extension | Format | Use Case |
|-----------|--------|----------|
| `.agent.yaml` | YAML | Human-edited configs (supports comments, multiline) |
| `.agent.yml` | YAML | Shorthand alternative |
| `.agent.json` | JSON | Programmatically generated configs |

### Discovery Behavior

`discoverAgentConfigFiles(path)` operates in two modes:

1. **Directory path** — scans entries (non-recursive) and returns all matching files
2. **File path** — returns the file in an array if it matches, otherwise empty array

```typescript
// Scan a directory
const agents = discoverAgentConfigFiles('./agents/');

// Validate a single file
const single = discoverAgentConfigFiles('./agents/researcher.agent.yaml');
```

The scan is intentionally non-recursive. If you need nested directories, call it multiple times or walk the tree yourself.

## Hot-Reload

When running in development with `kernova serve --watch`, agent config files are hot-reloaded automatically.

### How It Works

1. **Discovery** — `DaemonRunner` calls `discoverAgentConfigFiles(configPath)` at startup
2. **Watch setup** — `fs.watch` is attached to each discovered file and to the parent directory
3. **Change detection** — When a filesystem event fires, it's debounced (100ms) to batch rapid saves
4. **Re-parse** — The changed file is re-parsed with `loadAgentConfigWithExtends()`
5. **Re-register** — The kernel's agent registry is updated with the new definition
6. **Error handling** — Parse errors are logged but don't crash; the previous agent definition stays active

### Lifecycle Events

| Filesystem Event | Action |
|-----------------|--------|
| File modified | Debounce → re-parse → re-register agent |
| File deleted | Unregister the agent from the kernel |
| New file created | Parse → register as a new agent |
| Parse error | Log error, keep previous definition active |

### Example Development Workflow

```bash
# Terminal 1: Start with hot-reload
kernova serve --watch

# Terminal 2: Edit an agent
vim agents/researcher.agent.yaml
# Save → "Agent 'researcher' reloaded" appears in Terminal 1
```

```typescript
// Programmatic equivalent
import { watchAgentConfigFiles, discoverAgentConfigFiles, loadAgentConfigWithExtends } from '@kernova/core';

const configDir = './agents/';
const files = discoverAgentConfigFiles(configDir);

let debounceTimer: NodeJS.Timeout | null = null;

const stop = watchAgentConfigFiles(files, (filePath, event) => {
  if (debounceTimer) clearTimeout(debounceTimer);

  debounceTimer = setTimeout(() => {
    try {
      const config = loadAgentConfigWithExtends(filePath);
      kernel.agentRegistry.reregister(config);
      console.log(`Agent '${config.name}' reloaded`);
    } catch (err) {
      if (err instanceof AgentConfigError) {
        console.error(`Config error: ${err.message}`);
        // Previous agent definition stays active
      }
    }
  }, 100);
});
```

## Validation Rules

All config files are validated on parse. Invalid configs throw `AgentConfigError` with a descriptive message.

### Required Fields

| Field | Rule |
|-------|------|
| `name` | Must be a non-empty string |
| `instructions` | Must be a non-empty string |

### Optional Field Validation

| Field | Rule |
|-------|------|
| `description` | If present, must be a string |
| `model` | If present, must be a string |
| `tools` | If present, must be an array of strings |
| `extends` | If present, must be a string (relative path) |
| `schedules` | If present, must be an array of schedule objects |
| `triggers` | If present, must be an array of trigger objects |

### Schedule Object Validation

| Field | Required | Rule |
|-------|----------|------|
| `name` | Yes | Non-empty string |
| `goal` | Yes | Non-empty string |
| `cron` | No | String (5-field cron format, e.g., `"0 * * * *"`) |
| `delayMs` | No | Number (milliseconds) |

### Trigger Object Validation

| Field | Required | Rule |
|-------|----------|------|
| `name` | Yes | Non-empty string |
| `event` | Yes | Non-empty string (glob pattern, e.g., `"intent.failed"`) |
| `goal` | Yes | Non-empty string |
| `condition` | No | String (JavaScript expression evaluated at runtime) |

### Error Examples

```typescript
import { parseAgentConfigFile, AgentConfigError } from '@kernova/core';

try {
  parseAgentConfigFile('./broken.agent.yaml');
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof AgentConfigError) {
    console.error(err.message);
    // "[AgentConfig] /abs/path/broken.agent.yaml: Missing or invalid required field 'name' (must be a non-empty string)"
    console.error(err.filePath);
    // "/abs/path/broken.agent.yaml"
  }
}
```

---

## AgentConfigError

Custom error class thrown for any config file issue — missing fields, parse errors, circular extends, file not found.

```typescript
class AgentConfigError extends Error {
  /** Descriptive error text (prefixed with file path) */
  message: string;

  /** Absolute path to the file that caused the error */
  filePath: string;

  /** Always 'AgentConfigError' — useful for instanceof checks */
  name: 'AgentConfigError';
}
```

### Common Error Scenarios

| Scenario | Message Pattern |
|----------|----------------|
| File not found | `File not found` |
| Invalid JSON | `Invalid JSON: Unexpected token...` |
| Invalid YAML | `Invalid YAML: ...` |
| Missing name | `Missing or invalid required field 'name'` |
| Missing instructions | `Missing or invalid required field 'instructions'` |
| Bad tools array | `Field 'tools' must be an array of strings` |
| Circular extends | `Circular extends dependency detected` |
| Schedule missing goal | `schedules[0].goal is required and must be a string` |

## Events

ConfigManager emits events through the kernel's event bus when configuration changes.

| Event | When Emitted | Data |
|-------|-------------|------|
| `config.changed` | A value changes in any layer (via `set()` or `reload()`) | `{ path, value, layer }` or `{ path, oldValue, newValue, layer }` |
| `config.reloaded` | `reload()` is called with new file config | `{ changeCount }` |

### Subscribing to Config Events

```typescript
kernel.eventBus.subscribe('config.changed', (event) => {
  const { path, value, layer } = event.data;
  console.log(`[${layer}] ${path} = ${value}`);
});

kernel.eventBus.subscribe('config.reloaded', (event) => {
  console.log(`Config reloaded: ${event.data.changeCount} changes`);
});
```

### Change Detection

On `reload()`, ConfigManager diffs the previous file config against the new one. Only paths with actual value changes emit `config.changed` events. If nothing changed, `config.reloaded` still fires with `changeCount: 0`.

## Best Practices

### Choose the Right Format

- **YAML** for human-edited configs — supports comments, multiline strings with `|`, and is easier to read
- **JSON** for programmatically generated configs — easier to produce from code, no indentation ambiguity

### Environment Variables for Secrets

Never put API keys or credentials in config files. Use the env layer:

```bash
# .env (not committed to git)
KERNOVA_MODELS__DEFAULT__PROVIDER=openai
OPENAI_API_KEY=sk-...
```

```yaml
# kernova.config.json (committed to git) — no secrets here
{
  "models": {
    "default": { "model": "gpt-4o" }
  }
}
```

### Keep Base Configs Minimal

Base configs should contain only what's truly shared. Specialize in child configs:

```yaml
# base.agent.yaml — minimal shared defaults
name: base
instructions: |
  You are part of the Kernova system.
  Always be professional and concise.
model: gpt-4o
```

```yaml
# researcher.agent.yaml — specialized
extends: ./base.agent.yaml
name: researcher
instructions: |
  You are a research specialist. Find accurate, sourced information.
tools:
  - web-search
  - http-fetch
```

### Validate Before Deploying

Use `parseAgentConfigFile()` in your CI/CD pipeline to catch config errors before deployment:

```typescript
// scripts/validate-agents.ts
import { discoverAgentConfigFiles, loadAgentConfigWithExtends } from '@kernova/core';

const files = discoverAgentConfigFiles('./agents/');
let errors = 0;

for (const file of files) {
  try {
    loadAgentConfigWithExtends(file);
    console.log(`✓ ${file}`);
  } catch (err) {
    console.error(`✗ ${file}: ${(err as Error).message}`);
    errors++;
  }
}

if (errors > 0) {
  console.error(`\n${errors} config file(s) failed validation.`);
  process.exit(1);
}
```

### Runtime Override Patterns

Use `set()` for temporary overrides during testing or A/B experiments:

```typescript
// In tests
kernel.configManager.set('models.default.provider', 'mock');
kernel.configManager.set('models.default.model', 'mock-model');

// Feature flags
kernel.configManager.set('features.newPipeline', true);

if (kernel.configManager.get('features.newPipeline')) {
  // Use new pipeline
}
```

### Watch for Critical Changes

Set up watchers on paths that require re-initialization:

```typescript
kernel.configManager.watch('models.default.provider', (provider) => {
  // Re-initialize model client when provider changes
  modelClient = createModelClient(provider as string);
});

kernel.configManager.watch('gateway.port', (port) => {
  console.warn(`Port changed to ${port} — restart required for effect.`);
});
```

## Complete Example

A full project using both runtime config and declarative agent configs:

```
my-project/
├── agents/
│   ├── base.agent.yaml
│   ├── researcher.agent.yaml
│   └── writer.agent.yaml
├── kernova.config.json
├── src/
│   └── index.ts
└── package.json
```

```yaml
# agents/base.agent.yaml
name: base
instructions: |
  You are part of the Kernova system. Be accurate, helpful, and concise.
model: gpt-4o
```

```yaml
# agents/researcher.agent.yaml
name: researcher
extends: ./base.agent.yaml
description: Finds and synthesizes information from multiple sources
instructions: |
  You are a research specialist. When given a topic:
  1. Search for authoritative sources
  2. Cross-reference findings
  3. Summarize with citations
tools:
  - web-search
  - http-fetch
schedules:
  - name: daily-briefing
    cron: "0 9 * * *"
    goal: "Compile daily news briefing for subscribed topics"
```

```yaml
# agents/writer.agent.yaml
name: writer
extends: ./base.agent.yaml
description: Creates clear, engaging written content
instructions: |
  You are a writing specialist. Focus on clarity, structure, and engagement.
  Always use active voice and concrete examples.
tools:
  - http-fetch
triggers:
  - name: on-research-complete
    event: "agent.delegation.completed"
    goal: "Draft content from research findings"
    condition: "event.data.targetAgent === 'researcher'"
```

```typescript
// src/index.ts
import { KernovaKernel } from '@kernova/core';
import {
  discoverAgentConfigFiles,
  loadAgentConfigWithExtends,
  watchAgentConfigFiles,
  AgentConfigError,
} from '@kernova/core';

const kernel = new KernovaKernel({ environment: 'development' });
await kernel.start();

// Load all agent configs
const configDir = './agents/';
const files = discoverAgentConfigFiles(configDir);

for (const file of files) {
  try {
    const config = loadAgentConfigWithExtends(file);
    if (config.name === 'base') continue; // Skip abstract base
    kernel.registerAgentFromConfig(config);
    console.log(`Registered agent: ${config.name}`);
  } catch (err) {
    if (err instanceof AgentConfigError) {
      console.error(`Skipping ${err.filePath}: ${err.message}`);
    }
  }
}

// Watch for runtime config changes
kernel.configManager.watch('models.default.provider', (provider) => {
  console.log(`Model provider switched to: ${provider}`);
});

// Hot-reload agent configs in development
if (kernel.configManager.get('runtime.environment') === 'development') {
  watchAgentConfigFiles(files, (filePath, event) => {
    console.log(`Config ${event}: ${filePath}`);
    // DaemonRunner handles actual reload logic
  });
}
```

Kernova’s config system has two distinct subsystems that work together to configure your application at runtime and define agents declaratively.

SubsystemPurposePackage
ConfigManagerLayered runtime configuration with dot-path access, env overrides, change watching@kernova/core
Agent Config LoaderYAML/JSON agent definition files with inheritance, validation, discovery, hot-reload@kernova/core

Overview

Runtime configuration (ConfigManager) handles your application’s settings — model provider, ports, budgets, feature flags. It resolves values through a priority chain: hardcoded defaults → file config → environment variables → programmatic overrides. Any layer can be changed at runtime, and watchers fire when values change.

Agent config files are declarative .agent.yaml / .agent.yml / .agent.json files that define agents without writing TypeScript. They support extends inheritance, are validated on load, and can be hot-reloaded during development. The CLI’s kernova serve --watch picks up changes automatically.

Both systems are exported from @kernova/core:

Runtime Configuration (ConfigManager)

Layer Priority

ConfigManager resolves values through four layers, highest priority first:

PriorityLayerSourceTypical Use
1 (highest)runtimeSet programmatically via .set()Feature flags, temporary overrides
2envEnvironment variables with KERNOVA_ prefixSecrets, deployment-specific values
3fileLoaded from kernova.config.jsonProject defaults, shared team settings
4 (lowest)defaultsHardcoded in codeSafe fallbacks

When you call .get('models.default.provider'), ConfigManager checks each layer top-to-bottom and returns the first defined value.

Initialization

ConfigManager is created by the kernel during startup. You can also instantiate it directly:

API Reference

get<T>(path): T | undefined

Resolve a value through all layers using dot-path notation.

getOrDefault<T>(path, defaultValue): T

Same as get() but returns a fallback if no layer has the value.

set(path, value): void

Set a runtime override. This is the highest-priority layer — it wins over env, file, and defaults.

Setting a value also triggers watchers and emits a config.changed event.

reload(fileConfig): void

Replace the file layer entirely. Useful after detecting a config file change on disk.

After reload, a config.reloaded event is emitted with the number of changed paths.

watch(path, callback): () => void

Subscribe to changes for a specific config path. Returns an unsubscribe function.

Watchers fire when:

  • set() is called with a new value for that path
  • reload() is called and the file layer has a different value at that path

getAll(): Record<string, unknown>

Get the fully merged configuration object (all layers combined, higher priority wins).

Environment Variable Mapping

Environment variables are mapped to config paths using a prefix and double-underscore nesting:

Environment VariableConfig Path
KERNOVA_MODELS__DEFAULT__PROVIDERmodels.default.provider
KERNOVA_GATEWAY__PORTgateway.port
KERNOVA_RUNTIME__DEBUGruntime.debug

Rules:

  • Prefix: KERNOVA_ (configurable via envPrefix option)
  • Nesting separator: __ (double underscore) → converted to . in config paths

When getAll() merges layers, it uses deep merge for objects and replacement for scalars/arrays:

  • Objects — recursively merged (keys from higher-priority layers override lower)
  • Scalars — replaced entirely
  • Arrays — replaced entirely (not concatenated)

Agent config files let you define agents declaratively without writing TypeScript. They’re ideal for prompt iteration, non-developer authoring, and version-controlled agent definitions.

Config Inheritance (extends)

The extends field lets an agent config inherit from a base config. This is useful for sharing instructions, model choices, or tool sets across multiple agents.

How It Works

  1. The loader reads the child config file
  2. If extends is present, it resolves the path relative to the child file’s directory
  3. The base config is loaded (recursively — bases can extend other bases)
  4. The child is merged on top of the base

How Kernova assembles context for agents — five-layer memory, context computation, pluggable context engines, conversation threads, and RAG retrieval.

Agents are only as good as the context they receive. Without memory of who’s asking, what they already know, and what’s relevant to the current task, even the most capable model produces generic, unhelpful responses. Kernova solves this with a multi-layered memory system and a context computation pipeline that assembles the right information for every intent — automatically.

This guide covers the five tightly-coupled modules that power Kernova’s context system:

  • MemoryEngine — 5-layer persistent memory with FTS5 full-text search and vector embeddings
  • ContextEngine — computes context from memory layers for each intent
  • ContextEngineManager — pluggable architecture for custom context strategies
  • ConversationManager — named threads with sliding window and summarization
  • RAGPipeline — document ingestion and semantic retrieval

Overview

The Problem

Every time an agent receives a goal, it needs to know: who is asking (identity, preferences), what they already know (conversation history), and what’s relevant (domain knowledge, documentation). Without these answers, agents hallucinate, repeat themselves, and ignore user context.

Kernova’s Answer: Context Is Computed, Not Stored

Kernova doesn’t store a single “context blob” that grows forever. Instead, context is assembled fresh for each intent from multiple sources. This means context is always relevant, within token budgets, and reflects the latest memory state.

The Pipeline

When an intent arrives, the context assembly pipeline runs automatically:

  1. Intent arrives → ContextEngine queries MemoryEngine across all layers
  2. ComputedContext assembled → Memories prioritized, deduplicated, token-counted
  3. RAG enrichment → Relevant document chunks retrieved and appended
  4. Conversation context → Thread summary and recent messages included
  5. Agent receives full context → Everything packaged as ComputedContext

This happens transparently on every kernel.submit() call.

Memory Engine (5 Layers)

The MemoryEngine is Kernova’s persistent knowledge store. It organizes memories into five layers, each with a distinct purpose and lifecycle. This layered architecture ensures that short-lived task notes don’t pollute long-term user preferences, and organizational knowledge doesn’t expire with a session.

Layer Architecture

LayerPurposeTTLExample
workingCurrent task scratchpadMinutes”Currently analyzing file X”
sessionCurrent conversation contextHours (3600s default)“User asked about deployment”
longtermPersistent user knowledgeMonths/years”User prefers TypeScript”
organizationalShared team knowledgeIndefinite”Company uses PostgreSQL”
globalSystem-wide factsIndefinite”The API base URL is…”

Layer priority (highest to lowest): working → session → longterm → organizational → global. Higher-priority layers override lower ones during context assembly.

Storing Memories

Each memory entry includes:

  • content — The information to remember (string)
  • layer — Which memory layer to store in
  • tags — Categorization labels for filtering
  • owner — The user or entity this memory belongs to
  • relevance — Relevance score (0.0–1.0, defaults to 1.0)
  • confidence — Certainty score (0.0–1.0)

Querying Memories

Search Capabilities

The memory engine provides three search modes:

  • FTS5 Full-Text Search — Keyword-based matching using SQLite’s FTS5 engine. Fast and exact.
  • Vector Embeddings — Semantic similarity via the ModelRouter. Finds conceptually related memories even when keywords don’t match.
  • Hybrid Mode (default) — Tries semantic search first, falls back to FTS5 if unavailable.

Filtering Options

Memory Decay

Memories don’t stay equally relevant forever. Memory decay gradually reduces relevance scores of older memories, letting fresh information naturally surface above stale data.

Run decay on a schedule (daily or hourly) to keep your memory store fresh. Memories that are re-confirmed (re-stored with same content) reset their relevance to 1.0, naturally resisting decay.

Context Computation

The ContextEngine is the bridge between raw memories and actionable agent context. For every intent, it queries the memory engine across all layers, prioritizes results, and packages them into a structured ComputedContext.

Context Assembly Sequence

  1. Query working memory for the owner (limit: 10)
  2. Query session memory for the owner (limit: 20)
  3. Query longterm memory with the goal as search text (limit: 10)
  4. Query organizational memory with the goal (limit: 5)
  5. Combine with priority: working > session > longterm > organizational
  6. Estimate token count and trim if needed
  7. Return ComputedContext

The ComputedContext Interface

Token Budget Management

The context engine is token-aware. It estimates token count and ensures context doesn’t exceed model limits:

  1. Lower-priority memories are dropped first (organizational before longterm)
  2. Within a layer, lower-relevance memories are dropped first
  3. The estimatedTokens field reflects the final assembled size

Agents never receive context that would blow their token window — the engine handles truncation intelligently.

Pluggable Context Engines

The default context engine works for most applications. For specialized context assembly — external vector databases, domain-specific ranking, or proprietary knowledge systems — the ContextEngineManager provides a plugin architecture.

Conversation Threads

The ConversationManager provides named threads with sliding-window management and LLM-powered summarization — conversational continuity without unbounded context growth.

Creating and Using Threads

Getting Thread Context

Sliding Window Mechanics

  • Default window size: 50 messages
  • When exceeded: Oldest messages beyond the window are summarized using the LLM
  • Summary prepended: Agents see the summary before the recent messages
  • Recent preserved in full: Messages within the window are never truncated

A 200-message conversation still fits within token limits — the agent sees a summary of messages 1–150 and full content of messages 151–200.

RAG Pipeline

The RAGPipeline handles document ingestion, chunking, embedding, and retrieval — giving agents access to your documentation and knowledge bases without stuffing everything into the prompt.

Ingesting Documents

Chunking Strategies

The RAG pipeline supports four chunking strategies:

StrategyBehaviorBest For
fixedSplit every N tokens regardless of contentUniform chunk sizes, simple docs
recursiveSplit on headers, paragraphs, then sentencesDefault — Markdown, technical docs
sentenceSplit on sentence boundariesProse, articles, natural text
paragraphSplit on paragraph boundariesWell-structured documents

The recursive strategy (default) respects document structure — splits at headers first, then paragraphs, then sentences — producing semantically coherent chunks.
