Best Practices

Memory Best Practices

  • Use longterm for persistent facts — preferences, project info, learned patterns
  • Use session for current-task context — auto-expires, no cleanup needed
  • Use working sparingly — very short-lived, immediate task scratchpad only
  • Run decay() on a schedule — daily/hourly keeps memory fresh
  • Use tags consistently — establish a taxonomy (preference, fact, task, finding)
  • Store atomic facts — one fact per entry, not paragraphs of mixed information

Conversation Thread Best Practices

  • One topic per thread — keeps context focused
  • Descriptive thread IDs — support-ticket-123 over thread-1
  • Archive completed threads — preserve for potential memory extraction
  • Sub-threads for complex tasks — deployment thread doesn’t need code review messages

RAG Best Practices

  • Ingest at startup — load core documentation when the kernel starts
  • Use metadata — categorize documents for filtered retrieval
  • Keep documents fresh — re-ingest when docs change
  • Use recursive chunking for Markdown — respects headers and structure

Context Engine Best Practices

  • Trust the defaults — the built-in engine handles most applications well
  • Monitor estimatedTokens — if consistently near budget, be more selective with storage
  • Use custom engines for scale — external vector DBs for thousands of documents or millions of memories

Anti-Patterns

  • ❌ Storing entire conversations as a single memory (store individual facts)
  • ❌ Using longterm for ephemeral information (use session instead)
  • ❌ Creating one thread per message (one thread per conversation)
  • ❌ Ingesting huge files without chunking (let RAG handle splitting)
  • ❌ Never running decay (old memories dilute relevance)

Run Kernova as a persistent background service — signal handling, heartbeat, agent config loading, hot-reload, and graceful shutdown.

Most applications need Kernova to start, stay running, and shut down cleanly — surviving deploys, handling restarts, and loading agent configurations from disk without downtime. Daemon mode wraps the kernel in a production-ready lifecycle manager that handles all of this automatically.

The DaemonRunner (from packages/core/src/daemon/index.ts) is a thin wrapper over KernovaKernel that adds:

  • Signal handling — Catches SIGINT and SIGTERM for graceful shutdown
  • Heartbeat emission — Periodic health pulse with uptime and active intent counts
  • Agent config loading — Reads agent definitions from YAML/JSON files on disk
  • Hot-reload — Watches config files for changes and re-registers agents without restart
  • Graceful shutdown — Waits for active intents to complete before stopping the kernel

When to Use Daemon Mode

Use daemon mode when:

  • Running Kernova as a long-lived background service (servers, workers, cron hosts)
  • Deploying with systemd, Docker, PM2, or any process manager that sends signals
  • Managing agents via config files that ops teams can edit without code changes
  • You need zero-downtime agent updates via hot-reload

For short-lived scripts, tests, or serverless functions, use the kernel directly without the daemon wrapper.

Agent Config Loading

The daemon loads agent definitions from YAML or JSON config files at startup. This allows ops teams to manage agents without touching application code.

Single File

Directory (Multiple Agents)

The daemon uses discoverAgentConfigFiles() to find all valid agent config files in the path. It supports the extends field for config inheritance — a base config can define shared tools and instructions that specialized agents extend.

Loading Behavior

  1. Each config file is parsed with loadAgentConfigWithExtends() (resolves inheritance)
  2. A defineAgent() call creates the agent definition and executor
  3. The agent is registered with the kernel’s agentRegistry
  4. Schedules and triggers from the config are registered with the kernel’s scheduler and trigger system
  5. Each agent gets a stable ID (config-agent-{name}) for hot-reload re-registration

Error Handling

If a config file fails to parse, the daemon:

  • Emits a daemon.config.error event with the file path and error message
  • Skips that file and continues loading the rest
  • Does not crash or stop other agents from loading

Inspecting Loaded Configs

Hot-Reload

When watch: true, the daemon monitors config files for changes and automatically re-registers agents without restarting the process.

What Gets Watched

  • Individual config files — Each discovered .agent.yaml / .agent.json file
  • Parent directory — Detects new files added or existing files deleted

Debouncing

File change events are debounced per-file with a 100ms window. Rapid saves (e.g., editor auto-save) trigger only a single reload.

Change Scenarios

ScenarioBehavior
File modifiedRe-parse, re-register agent with same stable ID
File deletedUnregister agent from kernel, emit daemon.agent.unregistered
New file addedDetect via directory watcher, parse and register new agent
Parse error on changeKeep old agent definition active, emit daemon.config.error
Agent renamed in fileUnregister old name, register under new name

Parse Error Safety

Hot-reload is safe by default. If a modified config file has a syntax error or invalid structure, the daemon keeps the previous working definition active and emits an error event. Your agents never go down because of a typo in a config edit.

Best Practices

Shutdown Timeout

  • Set shutdownTimeoutMs based on your longest expected intent execution time
  • Add a buffer to your process manager’s stop timeout (e.g., shutdownTimeoutMs + 5000)
  • If intents regularly timeout, investigate why they’re slow rather than increasing the timeout

Hot-Reload

  • Keep agent config files in version control — deploy changes via git pull + file system update
  • Test config changes in staging before deploying to production
  • Monitor daemon.config.error events — they indicate broken configs that didn’t take effect
  • Parse errors are safe (old definition stays active), but they still need fixing

Heartbeat

  • Use heartbeat events to drive external health checks and monitoring dashboards
  • A missing heartbeat (no event within 2× the interval) indicates the daemon is stuck or crashed
  • Keep the interval reasonable — 30–60s for production, shorter for debugging

Config File Organization

Signal Handling

  • Never call process.exit() directly — let the daemon handle shutdown cleanly
  • The daemon removes its own signal handlers during shutdown to avoid double-invocation
  • If you need custom shutdown logic, subscribe to daemon.stopping rather than adding your own signal handlers

Monitoring Checklist

Anti-Patterns

  • ❌ Running multiple daemon instances with the same dataDir — SQLite lock contention
  • ❌ Using watch: true with network-mounted config directories — unreliable fs events
  • ❌ Ignoring daemon.config.error events — broken configs go unnoticed
  • ❌ Very short heartbeat intervals (< 5s) — unnecessary event bus noise

Every request in Kernova has an owner. Before an intent reaches an agent, before a tool executes, before a single token is generated — the kernel asks three questions: Who are you? (Identity), Should we believe you? (Permissions), and What can you touch? (Sandbox). This guide covers the six modules that answer those questions and how they work together to keep your system secure.

The security stack is composed of:

  • IdentityManager — Registers and authenticates users, agents, and services
  • ApiKeyManager — Generates and validates scoped API keys
  • SessionManager — Token-based sessions with TTL and invalidation

The event-driven nervous system of Kernova — pub/sub, wildcard patterns, persistent storage, querying, timelines, and retention policies.

Every state change in Kernova flows through the EventBus. When an intent is submitted, an agent completes a step, a memory is stored, or a tool executes — an event is published. This makes the entire runtime observable, auditable, and reactive.

The EventBus operates in dual mode:

  • In-memory pub/sub — Real-time delivery to active subscribers with a hot cache
  • Persistent storage — SQLite-backed history for querying, timelines, and replay

Event Structure

Every event follows the KernovaEvent interface. Events are immutable once created.

Publishing Events

The kernel publishes events automatically for all internal state changes. You can also publish custom events through the bus.

Events are delivered synchronously to subscribers and buffered for async persistence to SQLite. The publish() call never blocks on disk writes.

*.createdintent.created, agent.createdintent.completed

Wildcards match exactly one segment — intent.* won’t match intent.step.done.

Event Persistence

When persistence is enabled (the default), all events are stored in SQLite with batched writes.

How it works:

  1. Event lands in the hot cache and write buffer
  2. Buffer accumulates events (default batch size: 100)
  3. When the buffer fills or the flush timer fires (every 1s), events write in a single transaction
  4. Queries flush pending events first so results always reflect the latest state

Storage configuration:

  • WAL mode for concurrent read/write performance
  • Indexes on subject_id, event_type, correlation_id, timestamp, category
  • JSON columns for flexible data and metadata payloads

Decompose complex goals into steps, evaluate output quality with self-reflection, and ground responses in documents with retrieval-augmented generation.

Simple prompts work for simple tasks. But when an agent needs to accomplish something complex — researching a topic, generating a multi-part deliverable, or answering questions grounded in your documentation — a single LLM call isn’t enough. Kernova provides three intelligence modules that elevate agent capabilities from “chat completions” to structured cognitive work:

  • AgentPlanner — Decomposes complex goals into ordered steps and executes them adaptively
  • SelfReflection — Evaluates agent output against quality criteria and revises until it passes
  • RAGPipeline — Ingests documents, chunks them, and retrieves relevant context for queries

These modules work independently or compose together: RAG provides grounding context, the planner breaks goals into manageable steps, and reflection ensures each output meets quality standards before it reaches the user.

Agent Planner

The AgentPlanner implements the plan-and-execute pattern — a proven approach where complex goals are decomposed into steps before execution begins. Instead of asking an LLM to solve everything in one shot, the planner:

  1. Decomposes the goal into ordered, actionable steps via the LLM
  2. Executes each step sequentially using a provided executor function
  3. Replans adaptively when a step fails, generating alternative steps

This pattern works because LLMs produce better results on focused, narrow tasks than on broad, multi-faceted goals.

Quick Start

API Reference

plan(goal, context?)

Decomposes a goal into an ordered list of steps using the LLM.

Parameters:

  • goal (string, required) — The high-level objective to decompose
  • context (string, optional) — Additional context to inform step generation

Returns: ExecutionPlan with status 'planning' and generated steps.

execute(plan, executor)

Runs a plan step-by-step, calling the executor function for each step.

Parameters:

  • plan (ExecutionPlan, required) — The plan to execute (from plan())
  • executor (StepExecutor, required) — Async function called for each step

Returns: The updated ExecutionPlan with final status and step results.

The executor receives the current step and the full plan. If the executor throws, the step is marked as failed and adaptive replanning kicks in (if enabled).

cancel(planId)

Cancels an active plan. Pending steps are marked as skipped.

getPlan(planId) / listPlans()

Retrieve active plans for inspection or monitoring.

Adaptive Replanning

When a step fails, the planner doesn’t give up immediately. With adaptiveReplanning: true (the default), it asks the LLM to generate alternative steps that work around the failure:

Replanning is limited by maxReplanAttempts (default: 2) to prevent infinite retry loops. If replanning also fails or produces no alternatives, the plan status becomes 'failed'.

Self-Reflection

The SelfReflection module gives agents the ability to evaluate their own output and iteratively improve it. After an agent produces a response, reflection scores the output against configurable criteria (accuracy, completeness, clarity) and triggers revision if the score falls below threshold.

This is wired into Kernova’s execution pipeline — when reflection is enabled, it runs automatically after every agent produces output. No manual intervention required.

How It Works

Quick Start

API Reference

reflect(output, goal, context?, agentId?)

Full reflection cycle: evaluate, then revise iteratively until quality passes or max attempts reached.

Parameters:

  • output (string, required) — The agent’s output to evaluate
  • goal (string, required) — The original goal that produced the output
  • context (string, optional) — Additional context for evaluation
  • agentId (string, optional) — Agent identifier for event correlation

Returns: ReflectionResult containing:

Evaluate an output without triggering the revision loop. Useful for scoring/grading.

Configuration

Global Configuration

Per-Agent Configuration

Per-agent config overrides global settings. An agent can opt out of reflection even when it’s globally enabled, or configure a stricter threshold:

Resolution rules:

  • Global enabled: false + agent doesn’t specify → reflection is off
  • Agent enabled: true → overrides global disable
  • Agent enabled: false → overrides global enable
  • Agent threshold / maxAttempts → overrides global values when specified

Evaluation Criteria

The default criteria are ['accuracy', 'completeness', 'clarity']. Customize them globally or per-evaluation:

Graceful Fallback

If the LLM fails to produce a valid evaluation (network error, malformed response), reflection degrades gracefully:

  • Model failure during evaluation — Returns a neutral 0.5 score with “Could not parse evaluation” feedback
  • Model failure during revision — Keeps the original output
  • All attempts exhausted — Returns the best-scoring output seen across all attempts (not necessarily the last one)

The agent’s output is never lost. Worst case, the original output passes through unchanged.

When reflection is enabled, Kernova’s kernel execution pipeline automatically reflects on agent output:

RAG Pipeline

The RAGPipeline handles document ingestion, intelligent chunking, embedding generation, and semantic retrieval — giving agents access to your documentation and knowledge bases without stuffing everything into every prompt.

How It Works

Quick Start

API Reference

ingest(content, source, metadata?)

Ingest a document: chunk it according to the configured strategy and generate embeddings for each chunk.

Parameters:

  • content (string, required) — Full document text
  • source (string, required) — Identifier/filename for the document
  • metadata (Record<string, unknown>, optional) — Arbitrary metadata attached to chunks

Returns: Document object with generated id, source, and createdAt.

retrieve(query, options?)

Find relevant chunks for a query using semantic search with keyword fallback.

Parameters:

  • query (string, required) — The search query
  • options.topK (number, optional) — Maximum results to return (default: 5)
  • options.scoreThreshold (number, optional) — Minimum similarity score (default: 0.7)

Returns: RetrievalResult[] sorted by score descending:

getContext(query, options?)

Retrieve and format chunks into a single string ready for prompt injection.

remove(documentId) / clear()

Remove specific documents or clear the entire pipeline.

stats()

Get pipeline statistics.

Chunking Strategies

The RAG pipeline supports four chunking strategies, configured at initialization:

StrategyBehaviorBest For
fixedSplit at fixed token boundaries with overlapUniform sizes, unstructured text
recursiveSplit by paragraph → sentence → fixed (preserves structure)Default — Markdown, technical docs
sentenceGroup sentences until chunk budget is reachedProse, articles, natural language
paragraphGroup paragraphs until chunk budget is reachedWell-structured documents

The recursive strategy (default) is the most versatile — it respects document structure by trying larger splits first (paragraphs), then falling back to finer splits (sentences, then fixed) for oversized segments.

Search: Semantic + Keyword Fallback

The pipeline uses a two-tier search strategy:

  1. Semantic search (primary) — Embeds the query via the ModelRouter, computes cosine similarity against all chunk embeddings, and returns chunks above the score threshold.

  2. Keyword fallback — If embedding generation fails (model unavailable, network error), falls back to term-matching: splits the query into words and scores chunks by the fraction of query terms they contain.

This means RAG always works — even without an embedding model configured, you get basic keyword retrieval.

Best Practices

Planning

  • Keep goals specific — “Implement user auth with JWT” plans better than “Make the app secure”
  • Provide context — The more context the planner has, the more relevant the steps
  • Set appropriate maxSteps — Complex goals need more steps; simple goals should be capped low
  • Handle partial completion — Plans can hit maxSteps limit; design executors to handle partial results
  • Use events for monitoring — Subscribe to plan.step.failed and plan.replanned for observability

Reflection

  • Start with defaults — The 0.7 threshold and 2 max attempts work well for most use cases
  • Raise thresholds for critical output — Customer-facing content, legal text, or code generation may need 0.8+
  • Disable for speed-sensitive paths — Reflection adds 2-3 LLM calls; disable for real-time chat
  • Use evaluate() for analytics — Score outputs without revision to measure agent quality over time
  • Trust graceful fallback — If reflection fails, the original output passes through; this is by design

RAG

  • Ingest at startup — Load core documentation when the kernel starts, not on every query
  • Use recursive chunking for Markdown — It respects headers and structure

  • ❌ Ingesting entire codebases without filtering (dilutes retrieval quality)
  • ❌ Using reflection for deterministic outputs (code compilation, math — just validate directly)
  • ❌ Ignoring plan events (you lose visibility into why a plan failed)

Time-based jobs, priority task processing with retries, and event-driven rules — the three autonomy primitives that power always-on agents.

Autonomous agents need to act without being asked. They need to wake up on a schedule, process work reliably under load, and react to events the moment they happen. Kernova provides three primitives for this — each solving a distinct temporal problem:

  • Scheduler — “Do X at time Y” (cron jobs, delayed one-shots)
  • Task Queue — “Do X when capacity is available” (prioritized, retried, concurrent)
  • Proactive Triggers — “Do X when event Y happens” (pattern-matched, cooldown-enforced)

Together, these modules give agents full temporal autonomy: they can schedule future work, process it reliably, and chain reactions to outcomes — all without human intervention.

When to Use Each

PrimitiveUse WhenExample
SchedulerWork must happen at specific timesDaily reports, hourly syncs, delayed notifications
Task QueueWork must be processed reliably under loadEmail sending, data processing, API calls with retries
TriggersWork must happen in response to eventsReact to failures, chain workflows, alert on conditions

They compose naturally: a scheduled job enqueues tasks into the queue, and triggers react when those tasks complete or fail.

Scheduler

The Scheduler manages time-based job execution using setTimeout chaining for precise scheduling. It supports recurring cron jobs and one-shot delayed executions, with SQLite persistence and missed-execution detection on restart.

Cron Jobs (Recurring)

Standard 5-field cron expressions (minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week):

One-Shot Delayed Jobs

For work that should happen once after a delay (auto-disabled after execution):

One-shot jobs don’t retry — if you need retries, enqueue a task instead.

register(), remove(), list(), get()

Persistence & Missed Execution Detection

All jobs persist to SQLite ({dataDir}/kernova.db). On restart the scheduler loads all jobs, detects missed executions by comparing lastExecutionAt against the cron expression, emits scheduler.job.missed for each skipped tick, and schedules timers for all enabled jobs.

Overlap & Timeout

  • Overlap detection — If a cron job is still running when its next tick arrives, the execution is skipped and scheduler.job.skipped is emitted.
  • Execution timeout — Jobs are enforced with a max timeout (default: 300s). An AbortSignal is passed to the handler; when the timeout fires, the signal aborts and the job fails.

Task Queue

The TaskQueue provides prioritized async task execution with concurrency control, exponential backoff retries, and a dead-letter queue for exhausted tasks.

Priority Levels

Tasks are dequeued in strict priority order (FIFO within the same level):

PriorityUse For
criticalSystem-critical operations, incident response
highUser-facing tasks, time-sensitive work
mediumDefault — standard background processing
lowHousekeeping, analytics, non-urgent work

Concurrency Control

A semaphore limits parallel execution between 1 and 50 tasks (default: 5). This prevents resource exhaustion regardless of how many tasks are enqueued.

Registering Handlers

The signal is an AbortSignal — it fires on task timeout or graceful shutdown. Long-running handlers should check signal.aborted periodically.

Retry with Exponential Backoff

Failed tasks retry with: delay = min(baseDelay × 2^(attempt-1), maxDelay)

Defaults (baseDelay: 1000ms, maxDelay: 30000ms): 1st → 1s, 2nd → 2s, 3rd → 4s, 4th → 8s, 5th+ → 30s (capped). After exhausting maxRetries (default: 3), the task moves to the dead-letter queue.

Dead-Letter Queue & Replay

registerHandler(), enqueue(), stats(), deadLetters(), replay()

Graceful Shutdown

When stop() is called: stops accepting tasks → stops polling → waits up to shutdownTimeout for in-flight tasks → force-cancels remaining via AbortController → closes the store.

  • Separated by dots: intent.* matches intent.created but not intent.created.sub

Cooldown Enforcement

Minimum 100ms, default 1000ms. Events matching within the cooldown window after a fire are silently dropped:

Attach a runtime condition for fine-grained filtering. The trigger only fires when the condition returns true:

Conditions are runtime-only (not persisted). The conditionDescription string is stored for observability.

Best Practices

Scheduler:

  • Use cron for recurring work, one-shot for deferred single actions
  • Monitor scheduler.job.missed — indicates downtime during expected executions
  • Don’t put heavy logic in the scheduler callback — enqueue a task for reliability

Task Queue:

  • Register handlers before enqueueing — tasks without handlers fail immediately
  • Check signal.aborted in long-running handlers for clean cancellation
  • Set maxRetries per task type — idempotent tasks retry more; non-idempotent less
  • Monitor dead letters — they represent permanent failures needing investigation

Proactive Triggers:

  • Set cooldowns appropriate to the action — alerts need longer cooldowns than logging
  • Avoid trigger cascades — design patterns so trigger A’s events don’t re-fire trigger A
  • Re-register condition functions on restart — they’re closures, not persisted
  • Prefer disable() over remove() — disabled rules can be re-enabled

Anti-Patterns

  • ❌ Using the scheduler as a retry mechanism (use the queue’s built-in retries)
  • ❌ Setting cooldown below 100ms (validation rejects it)
  • ❌ Enqueueing tasks with no registered handler (immediate failure, no retry)
  • ❌ Ignoring dead-letter items (permanent failures need attention)
  • ❌ Creating triggers that react to their own action’s events (cascade loops)
  • ❌ Very short cron intervals with long-running jobs (overlap detection helps but redesign instead)

Build with the kernel API when you need full control — custom pipelines, advanced agent patterns, and direct subsystem access.

A complete working example that bypasses the SDK wrapper and uses @kernova/core directly. This gives you full control over the kernel lifecycle, raw access to every subsystem, and the flexibility to build custom frameworks, pipelines, or libraries on top of Kernova.

When to Use Core vs SDK

The SDK (@kernova/sdk) is the right choice for most applications — it starts the kernel for you, provides a fluent API, and handles lifecycle automatically. Use @kernova/core directly when:

  • You’re building a framework on top of Kernova (your own SDK, a SaaS platform, a multi-tenant system)
  • You need custom intent execution pipelines — preprocessing, routing, or post-processing that the SDK doesn’t support
  • You need direct subsystem access — raw EventBus subscriptions, manual memory management, programmatic scheduler control
  • You’re building a library that other developers import (you don’t want SDK opinions baked in)
  • You need multi-kernel setups — running multiple isolated kernel instances in a single process

### Quick Usage

```typescript
import { Kernova } from "@kernova/sdk";

const client = new Kernova({
  apiKey: process.env.KERNOVA_API_KEY,
  baseUrl: "http://localhost:3000",
});

// Health check
const status = await client.health();
console.log(status); // { status: "ok", version: "1.0.0" }

// Ask a single question
```

### Quick Usage

```go
package main

import (
    "context"
    "fmt"
    "log"

    kernova "github.com/kernova/kernova-go"
)

func main() {
    client := kernova.NewClient(
        kernova.WithAPIKey("your-api-key"),
        kernova.WithBaseURL("http://localhost:3000"),
    )

    ctx := context.Background()

    // Health check
    status, err := client.Health(ctx)
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(status.Status)

    // Ask a single question
    answer, err := client.Ask(ctx, &kernova.AskRequest{
        Prompt: "What is the capital of France?",
    })
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(answer.Text)

    // Multi-turn chat
    chat := client.Chat(ctx, &kernova.ChatOptions{Model: "default"})
    chat.Send("Hello, who are you?")
    reply, err := chat.Receive()
    if err != nil {
        log.Fatal(err)
    }
    fmt.Println(reply.Text)
}
```

### Notes

- Requires Go 1.21+
- Context-based cancellation and timeouts on every call
- Functional options pattern for client configuration
- Streaming via `client.AskStream()` returning a `<-chan kernova.Chunk`
- Zero external dependencies beyond the standard library

```rust
use kernova::Client;

async fn main() -> Result<(), kernova::Error> {
    let client = Client::builder()

        .base_url("http://localhost:3000")
        .build()?;

    // Health check

    println!("{}", reply.text);

    Ok(())
}
```

```java
            .apiKey("your-api-key")
            .baseUrl("http://localhost:3000")
            .build();

        // Health check
        HealthStatus status = client.health();
        System.out.println(status.getStatus());

        // Ask a single question
        AskResponse answer = client.ask("What is the capital of France?");
        System.out.println(answer.getText());

        // Multi-turn chat
        ChatSession chat = client.chat("default");
        chat.send("Hello, who are you?");
        ChatMessage reply = chat.receive();
        System.out.println(reply.getText());
    }
}
```

### Notes

- Requires Java 17+
- Built on `java.net.http.HttpClient` — no external HTTP dependencies
- Async variants return `CompletableFuture<T>` (e.g., `client.askAsync(...)`)
- Streaming via reactive `Flow.Publisher<Chunk>`
- Thread-safe client — create once, share across threads

## REST API (No SDK)

All SDKs wrap the same HTTP endpoints. If your language isn't listed, use any HTTP client:

```bash
# Health check
curl http://localhost:3000/api/health

# Ask a question
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/ask \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer your-api-key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"prompt": "What is the capital of France?"}'

# Chat (send message to session)
curl -X POST http://localhost:3000/api/chat \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer your-api-key" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"session_id": "abc123", "message": "Hello, who are you?"}'
```

## Common Configuration

All SDKs support these environment variables as defaults:

| Variable | Description |
|----------|-------------|
| `KERNOVA_API_KEY` | API key for authentication |
| `KERNOVA_BASE_URL` | Base URL of the Kernova instance |
| `KERNOVA_TIMEOUT` | Request timeout in milliseconds (default: 30000) |
| `KERNOVA_MAX_RETRIES` | Number of retries on transient failures (default: 3) |

When environment variables are set, you can create a client with no arguments:

```typescript
const client = new Kernova(); // reads from env
```

```python
client = Kernova()  # reads from env
```

```go
client := kernova.NewClient() // reads from env
```
